pr_body:
Schedules periodic timers relative to their previous absolute tick scheduled rather than the current time.

This seems to solve, for me, the unwanted behavior with intel_adsp timers where the mean time of the timer drifts into the future further than expected (and accumulates over the duration to be quite large, 400ms in this test).

Timer behavior test now gives me...


```
START - test_periodic_behavior
periodic timer behavior test
periodic timer samples gathered, calculating statistics
timer clock rate 38400000, kernel tick rate 50000, expected period 1000 us, samples 10000, period 38400.000000 cycles
statistics samples 10000, rollovers 0, mean 999.903211 us, variance 352.258525 us, stddev 18.768551 us, min 23.541667 us, max 1069.973958 us
statistics samples 10000, rollovers 0, mean 38396.283300 cycles, variance 519426.330441 cycles, stddev 720.712402 cycles, min 904 cycles, max 41087 cycles
timer start cycle 39861537, end cycle 423824370, total time 9999032.109375, expected time 10000000.000000, difference -967.890625
```

Which seems entirely reasonable.

Possibly Fixes #46378
pr_comments:
> @teburd my expectation to guarantee a synchronous use is that we do
> 
> ```c
> /* start the periodic timer */
> current = timer_get_cycles();
> timeout = current + period;
> timer_set_timeout(timeout);
> ```
> 
> and subsequent timeouts would be set as
> 
> ```c
> /* set the next timeout */
> timeout += period;
> timer_set_timeout(timeout);
> ```
> 
> We still need to check for valid timeout (i.e. not in past etc).
> 
> Can you confirm this is the case here ?
> 
> Doing above gives us a deterministic and synchronous tick for the workload.
> 
> Its up to the workload to deal with the scheduling latency (time it takes to run from timer cycle) and also leave some headroom to be guarantee that execution completes prior to the next tick.

That is indeed the goal. The min timer time in the test data above seems to be the first duration timer firing and probably the last_scheduled being incorrect for the first periodic timer. So there is indeed a short timer happening right at the beginning.
Tested on FPGA 50 and it helps a lot for glitches

No objection to merging this as a workaround, and I genuinely think the test is great (though for CI hygine maybe it could be a case in a different test vs. adding a new one?).  But I'm doubtful this is the root cause.

And I have to repeat that I was looking carefully at exactly this area in the spring and was really pretty certain things were fine at the time, implying that either something regressed or one of the fixes from that period got broken/mismerged or interacted with something else and isn't working.

Oh wait, have you checked @peter-mitsis 's fix from yesterday vs. this issue?  Indeed yes (if I'm remembering the symptom correctly) on the **last** k_timer handler in the list (IIRC SOF has only one, so "every time", I think) the announce_remaining value would get cleared before the handler and thus the uptime value seen in the handler would be, incorrectly, real time and not scheduled time.

Please test that vs. this rig.  I'll give it 60% odds that Peter already found the fix.

And FWIW: this also might explain why my rig in the spring didn't show it.  I think I was using a k_timer handler for each CPU, so the list wasn't ever being emptied by the handler iteration (each handler would re-add itself).

@andyross I don't disagree with what you are saying, k_uptime_ticks() should return the tick for which the timer was scheduled. After all we're getting the call back on that tick announce right? That's clearly I think the bug this is pointing towards, that its *not*. I don't love this fix, but it maybe (just like before) will point the way to where the issue is. I'm looking at this again and I think @peter-mitsis is correct here, and that fix would be nicer. This fix has some issues.
closing in favor of a better fix #48664
But the test is going to be resubmitted, or added as a case somewhere (maybe to timer_monotonic?) right?  It's a good test!

> But the test is going to be resubmitted, or added as a case somewhere (maybe to timer_monotonic?) right? It's a good test!

Yes, though probably in a week or so when I get back to fix the tick rounding drift scenario so nordic passes. Unless we want to think about fixing that as well? Like every so often shorten or lengthen the period by a tick to get the desired time period of the timer?

Could be done pretty easily I think (with some N digits of precision)

We could, but personally I think the value there is low vs. just documenting the existing behavior.  Some users want k_timer periods to be regular ("sample this device on a regular cadence" for data collection), some want them to be accurate vs. the wall clock.  A 32768 Hz timer can't do both.  No k_timer abstraction is going to insulate the users of those platforms from timer precision issues, so IMHO we shouldn't try and should just pick the simplest options where possible.

And in any case, users who want reliably corrected interrupts over time have absolute timeouts with which to do that; there exists a workaround already.

issue_context.title: CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC affects app code speed with tickless kernel
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
With CONFIG_TICKLESS_KERNEL=y build of Zephyr, we observe the SOF application code is running slower with a higher CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC setting. This is not the expected behavior for a tickless kernel.

**case A) CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC=15000**

[00007179] <inf> ll_schedule: ll timer avg 2022, max 2552, overruns 0

DSP load 5.27% (2022/38400*100%)

**case B) CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC=50000**

[00009227] <inf> ll_schedule: ll timer avg 2040, max 2792, overruns 0

DSP load 5.31% (2040/38400*100%)

So increasing the systick setting introduces a +0.2MCPS overhead to audio pipeline execution
in this case. The difference is not huge, but the expectation is no difference. 

**To Reproduce**
- Build SOF application with Zephyr (https://thesofproject.github.io/latest/getting_started/build-guide/build-with-zephyr.html). 
- play one audio stream 
- observe "ll_schedule: ll timer avg" in SOF application log

**Expected behavior**
No overhead to application execution from higher sys-clock-ticks-per-sec setting.

**Impact**
Not meeting performance target

**Logs and console output**
n/a

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - zephyr: a78e7c5c90d8cb31ec550ce289503bd698675585
 - sof: ebc222dab56868ea3cb0d5abec5057990eae6bb9
 - HW: Intel Tiger Lake cAVS2.5 system

**Additional context**
n/a
comments: @nashif  @fabiobaltieri  @ceolin I propose to bump the priority of this bug. With bug, https://github.com/thesofproject/sof/issues/5921 , the sys-tick setting also impacts the k_timer behaviour and this led to subtle but severe audio quality issues.

> @nashif @fabiobaltieri @ceolin I propose to bump the priority of this bug. With bug, [thesofproject/sof#5921](https://github.com/thesofproject/sof/issues/5921) , the sys-tick setting also impacts the k_timer behaviour and this led to subtle but severe audio quality issues.

The priority makes sense to me.

I've spent a few cycles looking into and thinking about this. I don't have a hard answer on it, but I do have a few thoughts.

At one level of analysis, it seems reasonable to expect to that raising CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC on a tickless kernel from 15000 to 50000 should not result in additional overhead. However, that does make certain assumptions.

Before getting to deep into them, I'd like to establish some baseline numbers. As I understand it, for tiger lake cavs, we have the following...

CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC=38400000

When the tick rate is at 15000 Hz each tick is about 2560 cycles (66.7 usec). When at 50000 Hz, each tick is about 768 cycles (20 usec). There are two immediate implications of this. The first is that the time at which a tick is delivered/announced may change. This can occur if timeouts are specified in milliseconds or microseconds and then converted to ticks. It is not clear to me if the application is doing this.

The second is that the change in granularity can in theory lead to more ticks being delivered (this will be application specific though). This can occur if there should be timer expirations between 20 usec and 66.7 usec apart from each other. Under the 15000 Hz scenario, they may get rolled together into the delivery of a single tick, while in the 50000 Hz scenario, being of finer granularity it could allow for the delivery of separate ticks. Again, it is not yet clear to me if this is applicable to the SOF application.

I'm going to present one other set of numbers. As mentioned in the issue, at 15000 Hz the average and max numbers were 2022 and  2552 respectively--a difference of 530. It is my understanding that these are measure in cycles. And at 50000 Hz those numbers were 2040 and 2792--a difference of 752. It is probably a coincidence, but I can't help but notice that 752 cycles is awfully close to 768--the time for one tick.

One other observation. The period in cycles at 15000 Hz is longer than the test's average time. And the period in cycles at 50000 is a bit more than a third of the test's average time.It may be a red herring, but my suspicion is that the change in granularity is giving rise to "extra" (as compared to the 15000 Hz case) ticks being delivered and processed.

Can someone more familiar with the SOF code provide some additional information?

SoF has its own scheduler concept on top of Zephyr, but the general idea is that there is a timer, that ticks every 1000usec and all the work is done within this time. On Xtos (the implementation without Zephyr) all the works is done from the interruption context and the timer is programmed to tick every 1000 usec. In other hand on Zephyr,  the timer interruption "just" wakes up other threads that, effectively, do the work that is not done in the interruption context. AFAIR, the timer interruption is not masked. 

The trick part is that SoF uses `TICKLESS_KERNEL`, and all the periodic ticks shouldn't happen. Assuming (just to simplify) that the only timer event is that one, we should have an timer interruption every 1000us only.

Thanks @peter-mitsis for the analysis. It indeed seems like a unlikely coincidence that the avg/max delta is so close to one tick. The 2040/2792 values are actually reads of the 38.4Mhz platform clock (behind k_cycle_get_32() on these platforms). The diff is measured over one 1000us tick, so difference of 752 cycles is 19.583usec, so indeed very close to the 20.000 usec of one 50kHz tick.

And ack @ceolin , SOF application indeed registers a k_timer() that fires every 1000us, and this is used to kick (with k_sem) threads to do the actual work. We can have occasional IPC or IDC irqs, but these do not happen in the stable state of this test where the measurement is made (a single stream is running and we just observe "stable state" performance). 

We also looked at the overall number of IRQs , and this seems to match with the intended design, e.g. nothing additional is fired between the 1000us k_timer ticks.

The race I believe I sorted out in my mind before in this code before goes with a flow like the following inside the adsp timer driver. Though was told there wasn't a race before, seeing this I'm less convinced.

Imagine the flow in intel_adsp_timer.c goes like the following.

core 0 takes driver lock, updates last count, releases driver lock and calls sys_clock_announce, takes k_timer lock
core 1 takes driver lock, updates last count, release driver lock and calls sys_clock_announce, waits on k_timer lock
core 0, takes the driver lock sets the next compare relative to the last count provided by core 1, releases driver lock.

Lock around the entire thing instead *or* only process the timer compare on one core and avoid the locks would be something I'd seriously consider trying. Though I believe there are issues with only processing the timer isr on one core for other task scheduling reasons from my recollection.

As a perhaps alternative entirely to using k_timer's where cycle precise application controller timer isrs are desired, a counter driver against the second timer compare could be provided directly enabling the application to set the timer compare value in cycles (counter ticks).

So I tried two things real quick with maybe more surprising results than I expected...

If I add an outter spin lock around the entire compare_isr call (including the announce) I lose *more* ticks.

If I bail early in compare_isr if (arch_curr_cpu()->id != 0) { return; } I get every tick exactly like I'd expect. Maybe some spin lock contention causing issues?

To add to my analysis above, the issue comes when core 1 updates the last_count (when the last announce occurred) while core 0 is still announcing. If core 1 happens to be a tick or more ahead, time is lost from the perspective of core 0 as it will potentially appear as if the announce took 1 or more ticks less than reality. This is more likely to occur when the tick rate is faster as the tick time period is shorter so the race is more likely to be seen.

Sneaking in:

> when core 1 updates the last_count (when the last announce occurred) while core 0 is still announcing. If core 1 happens to be a tick or more ahead

But... that's all correct.  There isn't a separate clock per core.  It's a single device.  If core 1 sees time as 1 tick ahead while core 0 is still announcing, that means that core 0 took more than one tick to finish the announce calls, by definition.  No time is being "lost", it's just slow.  No amount of timer architecture is going to make an ISR finish faster.

(FWIW: none of that explains the reported performance impact, though.  The ISR going longer than a tick is more common with high tick rates, but the performance impact is supposed to be the same regardless.)

Maybe the bug is on the other side?  Is the next timeout computation being done based on the "frozen" time when it really should be realtime?

We have the following call sequence executed in the timer expiration handler (z_timer_expiration_handler). Note that this handler is a callback routine called from within sys_clock_announce() in the context of the timer ISR.

`   k_uptime_ticks() -> sys_clock_tick_get() -> curr_tick + sys_clock_elapsed()
`

sys_clock_elapsed() simply does ...

`       uint32_t ret = (count32() - (uint32_t)last_count) / CYC_PER_TICK;`

What I think is happening is that when a the system clock rate is high, processing the timer ISR can be long enough that at least a tick's worth of time has elapsed. On a tickless kernel, this is not guaranteed to trigger the timer. However,  `sys_clock_elapsed()` can detect that time has passed. Unfortunately this is being done from within the context of the timer ISR and that tick has not yet been *announced*. This premature detection of the tick is leading to k_timer drift.

This can be fixed by modifying `sys_clock_tick_get()` to use `curr_tick + elapsed()` instead as `elapsed()` is designed to be used from within sys_clock_announce().

review_comments:
This is suspicious.  As mentioned in that comment, the current `k_uptime_ticks()` during a k_timer handler is supposed to be fixed at the time for which the timeout was scheduled (the reason is to prevent monotonicity bugs elsewhere in the system where e.g. interrupts that preempt this handler or threads running on other CPUs are seen to be "on a different timeline" in terms of event ordering, there was a long, long bikeshed about this during the timer rework c. 2018).

If that's not working, we probably have a bug somewhere else, I'm thinking.  Maybe start with an __ASSERT() here to make sure that we're firing when expected?  Maybe we can make this happen on an emulation platform by stuffing a busy wait in at the right moment?
